Benchmarks · The Hundred · mitts 0.3.17

One hundred Rust projects, measured.

Mitts and the two baselines a Rust developer actually has — plain cargo and cargo with sccache — run over the same open-source projects (100 on two machines, 90 on the third) on three machines. Every number below is a median of repeated runs, summarised across projects as a geometric mean. Where Mitts is not faster, the page says so.

6.9×faster than sccache when 12 worktrees of one project build at once (geometric mean over 100 projects, Apple M2 Ultra)
21×faster for the same code in a second worktree, because the first one already built it
≈1×on one cold build against plain Cargo. That case has nothing to reuse, so there is nothing to win; the numbers are below.

Results by scenario

Each bar is the geometric-mean speed-up of Mitts over a baseline across the projects of one machine. The axis is logarithmic: the vertical line is 1× (equal), bars to the right mean Mitts finished sooner, bars to the left mean the baseline did.

Against sccache

The best sound baseline: it caches compiler results and does not change them.

  • macOS · APFS · Apple M2 Ultra
  • Linux x86_64 · XFS · AMD Ryzen 9 9950X
  • Linux aarch64 · XFS

Against plain Cargo

A shared CARGO_TARGET_DIR is the other obvious shortcut. It is left out of the charts because it is unsound: in the recorded swarms it either missed the injected test failure or let it leak into clean worktrees. It is kept in the raw data as a demonstration.

The swarm: 12 worktrees at once

The scenario Mitts was built for. Twelve worktrees of one project, on four different commits, all build the project's tests at the same moment, the way parallel branches or coding agents do. Worktree 12 carries a deliberately failing test; an arm only counts as sound if it reports that failure and no other.

Every project, one point

Horizontal: seconds for sccache. Vertical: seconds for Mitts. A point under the diagonal means Mitts was faster on that project; hover for the name.

How the speed-up is spread

One tick per project on the same log axis; red ticks are projects where Mitts was slower.

Cold builds: where Mitts does not win

A single build of one checkout with empty caches has nothing to reuse. Against plain Cargo it is a tie by design, and on some projects Cargo is a little faster. Against sccache Mitts is about 1.4× faster on all three machines (the geometric means are in the tables). Speed-up of Mitts over plain Cargo, one tick per project:

Method

The Hundred
100 open-source Rust projects from crates.io and GitHub, fixed in scripts/corpus_100.json. nushell is excluded from this run. Projects Cargo itself cannot build are replaced so the corpus stays at 100.
Binary under test
mitts 0.3.17, commit 045c5cd241c0, release binary SHA-256 01408cb9aed29601fb20c7bfa2f1675c501dd6cbcf96defe4996eecb7eaed394. The latest release is newer; these numbers were not re-measured on it.
Baselines
Plain Cargo, Cargo + sccache (sccache 0.17.0), and a shared target directory demonstration. Cargo arms run --offline.
Scenarios
Fetch and plan (T0, T1); one cold build, no-op, edit one file, same code in a second worktree (T2); replay of 10 consecutive commits and branch switching (T3); check, clippy and reflink-versus-copy disk writes (T4); the 12-worktree swarm (T5).
Repeats
3 repeats per measurement; the median is used, with the quartiles kept in the raw data. Swarms use 12 worktrees on 4 commits.
Soundness
An arm's swarm counts only if every worktree builds, all arms produce the same number of test binaries, and the injected failing test in worktree 12 is reported. A swarm whose total time varies by more than 15% between repeats is flagged NOISY and kept out of every aggregate (chumsky, crc32fast, curve25519-dalek, dashmap, eza, fd, itoa).
Preflight
Before each run the machine must be quiet: CPU busy fraction and load below a threshold and no foreign compiler process, with the wait recorded. File systems are settled with sync before disk measurements.
Aggregation
Speed-up is baseline time divided by Mitts time per project; the summary is the geometric mean, with the count of projects where Mitts was faster and slower. The geometric mean is used because ratios multiply.
Provenance
Every result file records the binary hash, the hash of each script, the commit, the toolchain, the file systems and the load before each run. The raw reports, with absolute paths and device names removed, are published as benchmarks.json.

What these numbers do and do not say

  • One version. All three machines ran mitts 0.3.17. Mitts has changed since; each series stands on its own and numbers from different versions are not compared.
  • Warm caches favour Mitts by design. The swarm and second-worktree scenarios measure reuse. They show what a shared store buys when the same code is built many times, not what a single first build costs.
  • Build only. Test execution time belongs to the tests and is identical for every arm, so the swarm runs test --no-run. Soundness is checked with two short executions that never enter the metric.
  • Three repeats. Medians of three runs are stable for these workloads but not a confidence interval. The quartiles are in the data.
  • Desktop noise. The Mac Studio carried resident agent sessions during its run. The gate records and bounds this; it does not remove it.
  • Disk figures. Device bytes written are whole-device counters and compare arms within one run, not across machines.
  • Not covered. Windows, cross-compilation and a remote or team cache are not supported yet and not measured.
